about_intro: Unseen Labyrinth is a strategic, card-based puzzle adventure that combines tactical movement with resource management. The player controls a knight who must navigate a constantly shifting labyrinth, whose paths rearrange with each turn. By playing cards, new routes can be opened or obstacles overcome, while limited turns and unpredictable changes add tension.
background_text: Unseen Labyrinth was created as part of the Druid Mechanics Game Jam 2025, hosted on itch.io. The theme of the jam was "What you don't see." Major inspirations for the core mechanics came from the classic board game "Labyrinth" and turn-based games such as "Hearthstone" and "Teamfight Tactics." Our goal was to develop a tactical game that combines the tension of a constantly changing labyrinth with the strategic use of cards.
story_text: As a knight, one ventures into a mysterious, fog-shrouded labyrinth to rescue a princess from her impending fate. Every step carries uncertainty, and each card can mean the difference between progress and a dead end – only those who plan tactically will reach her in time.
flow_text:
Each round consists of three phases. In the labyrinth phase, rows or columns are shifted, constantly rearranging the available paths. Afterward, the player automatically draws a card from the deck, which provides new tactical options. In the player phase, the knight can move freely along open paths – orthogonally and without step limits. Exactly one card may be played before ending the turn.

The interplay between the unpredictable labyrinth and the player’s deliberate actions demands constant adaptation and strategic decision-making. The knight must reach the princess within 30 turns, otherwise the game ends.
grid_text: The labyrinth is based on a procedurally generated 10×10 grid. Predefined tiles are distributed across the grid and randomly rotated, creating a new configuration with each run. The defining feature of the labyrinth is shifting. By shifting entire rows or columns are moved one step, with the displaced tile reappearing on the opposite side of the grid. This shifting constantly opens or blocks new routes. As in the board game, movement is restricted to orthogonal directions.
tiles_text: The tile types are also inspired by the board game: straights, corners, and T-junctions. Each tile starts covered in fog, functioning as a Fog of War similar to classic strategy games. Because of the fog, the princess’s position is unknown. Once the knight steps onto a tile, the fog is permanently lifted from it, even if the knight moves away or the labyrinth shifts later.
cards_text1: The cards feature a simple yet elegant design that fits into the fantasy/medieval setting. Each card uses symbols that clearly convey its function at a glance.
cards_text2: The card system allows the player to influence the labyrinth directly, creating meaningful tactical decisions. Each round, the player automatically draws one card. A maximum of seven cards may be held in hand at once. In each turn, exactly one card may be played, and any number of cards may be discarded. The deck is generated before the game begins and scales to the grid size.
cards_types: Within the jam scope, the following types were implemented: Reveal, Shift, Switch, Jump, Rotate.
playcard_intro: To play a card, it must first be selected in hand and then confirmed with the Play Card button. The card hand then fades out, and the camera switches to a top-down view for precise tile selection. The selection varies depending on the card type: Switch requires two tiles to swap, Rotate and Reveal require a single target tile, Jump allows selecting an adjacent orthogonal tile within the knight’s range, and Shift targets an outer tile to push the entire row or column. Using the Confirm button executes the action, after which the camera returns to the default view.
uiux_text: The interface draws inspiration from games with clear, intuitive interaction. Hearthstone influenced the readable card-hand design, while Teamfight Tactics inspired the round flow and phase communication. The goal was to build a UI that consistently communicates which phase is active, what actions are available, and how the player can interact.
phases_text: At the top of the screen, several elements indicate the current state: the phase display, the turn counter, and the "End Turn" button. The phase display cycles between "Labyrinth → Draw → Player." The turn counter shows the remaining number of turns. The "End Turn" button lets the player end their turn, starting the labyrinth phase.
cards_ui_flow_text: The card hand is displayed at the bottom of the screen. With the "Discard" button, selected cards can be removed. The "Play Card" button plays a card, switching the camera into a top-down view. Depending on the card, tiles can then be selected and confirmed with the "Confirm" button.

audio_art_text:
The sound design is minimalistic: a mysterious background track and distinct sound effects for important actions (steps, shifts, card actions).
Visually, the game uses a realistic fantasy/medieval style. The knight and princess are free assets from the Fab Store, as are the dungeon elements. Materials such as stone and metal and warm lighting accents provide orientation and atmosphere, while the UI remains deliberately minimalistic.
myrole_text:
My focus was on developing and integrating the game systems to create a structured yet dynamic flow. This included the turn and card system, the grid and labyrinth system with fog of war, and the UI/UX structure with phase display, card hand, and end-turn flow.
I initially built the systems independently and then merged them into a coherent prototype. This integration work was crucial for turning separate modules – grid logic, card actions, camera, and UI – into a cohesive gameplay experience. In addition to the technical work, I also coordinated collaboration, structured discussions, and documented results, ensuring efficient teamwork despite our simple setup.
The other two team members handled the dungeon design (tiles and characters) as well as the development of the core grid logic, including generation and shifting.
jam_eval_text: In the final evaluation of the Game Jam within the Druid Mechanics Community, which included a total of 35 submitted projects, we achieved first place in the category “Unique.” This result confirmed that our core idea and mechanics offered a distinctive approach, while also highlighting areas where the gameplay itself could be improved. Even though we did not win the overall prize, we are very happy with the outcome and the positive feedback we received.
reflection_text:
Collaboration throughout the project turned out to be both constructive and effective, especially during the game design phase. We were able to collect ideas, discuss pros and cons, and define a realistic MVP. Even though we relied only on a shared document for documentation and organization instead of tools like Jira, it still provided a clear basis for our work.

Building the systems modularly proved to be the right approach. I was able to develop the systems independently, and we could dynamically assign tasks. In the final phase, this meant extra effort for integration, but overall it provided a stable foundation.

There were also challenges. Differences in Unreal experience combined with varying availability of team members created hurdles. Additionally, the reduction of the group from five to three active members shortly after the project began limited the overall scope.

Several areas still offer optimization potential:
optimization_1: Bugs in the interaction between grid and character, especially after moving the knight through the labyrinth
optimization_2: Stronger limitation of the top-down view through fog, or full concealment of undiscovered tiles
optimization_4: Adjustment of the princess character model to better match the knight’s style
optimization_5: Clearer player guidance through tutorials, tooltips, or similar elements
reflection_text2: Even though not all details were polished, we were able to create a playable prototype in a short time that conveyed the core idea clearly. For me, this made the project a success, as I gained valuable hands-on experience in collaborative work with Unreal and improved my workflow within the engine.
